title: How do software (SaaS) companies make money, and what matters in their cases?
description: Subscription software economics for case interviews: ARR, churn, net revenue retention, CAC and LTV, with a worked customer lifetime value.
hook: Software-as-a-service businesses are now common in cases, especially in tech and private equity interviews. Their economics revolve around recurring revenue: win a customer once, keep them for years, and sell them more over time.
body:
The measures that matter

  • ARR (annual recurring revenue): the yearly value of all active subscriptions.
  • Churn: the share of customers who cancel.
  • Net revenue retention: what last year's customers pay this year, after cancellations, downgrades and upgrades.
  • CAC (customer acquisition cost) and LTV (lifetime value).

A worked example: is growth healthy?

A customer pays £100 a month at an 80% gross margin, so £80 a month of profit. Monthly churn is 2.5%, so customers stay about 40 months on average (1 ÷ 0.025). LTV ≈ £80 × 40 = £3,200. If winning a customer costs £1,200, LTV is about 2.7 times CAC, slightly below the common rule of thumb of 3. Cutting churn to 2% would lift lifetime to 50 months and LTV to £4,000.

Why retention matters so much

Net revenue retention above 100% means existing customers grow on their own, through upgrades and extra seats, even before any new sales.

Typical SaaS case questions

  • Why is churn rising?
  • Should we add a free plan? (a freemium question)
  • How should we price a new product tier?
  • Is this company a good private equity investment?
outro: Next in this topic: How do telecom companies make money, and what matters in a telecom case?
